title: Why Not Burn Him With a Look?
hook: the gods ask why the goddess didn't burn Mahisha with a glance, and find mercy in her sword
carry: the goddess is kind even to her enemies
tomorrow: two demon brothers take heaven. who do the gods remember?

segments.voice: Yesterday in the Devi Mahatmya, Mahisha changed shape again and again, until the goddess pinned him and he had to show himself.

If the goddess could end Mahisha with a single look, why fight at all? The gods themselves ask it. In the fourth chapter the buffalo is dead. The gods, Indra at their head, bow with necks bent and bodies thrilled, and praise her. Partway through their hymn they wonder out loud: you could have burned him to ash just by looking. Why didn't you? Their own answer is stranger. Today, the hymn, and the promise she leaves before she vanishes.
screen: `THE BATTLE IS OVER.` → `WHY NOT ONE LOOK?` → `A HYMN, AND A PROMISE.`

segments.voice: The hymn begins wide. In paraphrase, the gods bow to the goddess who spread out the whole world by her own power, whom even Vishnu, Shiva and Brahma can't fully describe. Then it comes into ordinary houses. She is good fortune in the homes of those who do good, and misfortune in the homes of those who do harm; understanding in the hearts of the learned, faith in the good, modesty in people of noble birth. In this hymn she isn't only on a battlefield. She's at the kitchen table, in what a house becomes. Then the question, and the gods answer it themselves. In paraphrase: so that the demons, purified by your weapons, might reach the higher worlds. Even toward enemies, your thought is kind. These demons had done enough harm to deserve a long time in hell, and you killed them in battle so they might reach heaven instead. In the gods' own hymn, the sword is a kind of mercy. Hindu stories say it again and again: an enemy who falls at the hand of the divine is set free, not thrown away. Then the goddess tells them to choose a boon. They say, in paraphrase: our enemy is dead, so everything is done. But if we remember you again, come and end our worst troubles, and may whoever praises you with this hymn prosper. She agrees, and vanishes. That promise is why many Hindus recite this text, or its verses, when trouble comes: remembered, she comes. The next chapter opens with new demons, and the gods, cornered again, remembering exactly this.
screen: `FORTUNE IN THE HOMES OF THE GOOD.` · `WHY NOT BURN HIM WITH A LOOK?` · `EVEN TOWARD ENEMIES, KIND.` · `REMEMBER ME, AND I WILL COME.` · then, large: `THE SWORD AS A KIND OF MERCY.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who has made life harder for you, not the hardest, just someone, and breathe with whatever rises. Then, without excusing anything they did, let one small wish form for their good, that they find some peace; you don't have to mean it completely. If you pray, hold them before God or the goddess in your own words; if you don't, let the wish ride out on the breath.
The Devi Mahatmya. Today, the gods' hymn: kindness even toward enemies, and a promise to come when remembered.
Your line: the goddess is kind even to her enemies. Even her sword, the hymn says, is mercy. Back tomorrow, same hill.

howItsDone: The gods' hymn in the fourth chapter of the Devi Mahatmya, sometimes called the Shakradi Stuti after Indra (Shakra), is recited as part of the whole text and is also chanted on its own by some devotees of the goddess.

original.note: Sanskrit: stuti, a hymn of praise. The fourth chapter is the gods' stuti to the goddess.

trapdoor: what you thought: a victory song after a battle.
what it means: the gods call her sword a mercy, kind even to enemies, an idea Hindu stories return to often; and her promise to come when remembered is why devotees recite this text in trouble.
what a scholar hears: chapter 4, the Shakradi Stuti, ending with the boon that the next chapter's gods remember when Shumbha and Nishumbha rise.

notes: Chapter 4 paraphrased: the gods led by Indra (Śakra) praise the goddess; she is fortune (śrī) in the dwellings of the virtuous and misfortune (alakṣmī) in those of the wicked, intelligence in the hearts of the learned, faith in the good, modesty in the high-born; why not reduce the demon to ashes by sight? so that, purified by her weapons, they may reach higher worlds; her mind is kind even to enemies; they had done enough evil to stay long in hell, but dying in battle they reach heaven. Confirm wording and that 'reach heaven' is fair.
The boon: whenever remembered again she will destroy the gods' worst calamities, and those who praise her with these hymns will prosper. Confirm.
